title: Latency-first SDK Canvas and Toolbound Protocol (PRD Draft)
content:
Purpose:
This doc proposes a ‘latency-first’ SDK canvas and a lightweight Toolbound Protocol for Hosted API clients. The aim is to make the common low-latency usage patterns (short-turn chat, micro-actions, mobile integrations) feel native to client teams while preserving the server-side guarantees we need for batching, KV caching, and safe tool invocation.

Background and problem framing:
- Many customers embed Redwood into UX-critical flows (search augmentation, in-app assistants, transactional helpers). They report inconsistent perceived latency when tool calls or structured validation happen mid-stream. Existing SDK surfaces bias either toward full fidelity (blocking tool calls > high latency) or eventual consistency (fire-and-forget > poor UX).
- Current hosted streaming APIs are powerful but require application teams to stitch: prefetching, local bundling, SDK-level buffering, and separate tool call orchestration. This increases product complexity for adopters and increases the number of partial-implementation anti-patterns we see in support.

Goals (what success looks like):
1) Perceived latency reduction for 95th percentile short-turn interactions by 30% in typical web and mobile clients (measured by RTT to first actionable token).
2) Provide a simple SDK surface where tool invocations can be declared, eagerly hinted, or deferred with minimal wiring.
3) Ensure server-side batching and prefix/KV caching remain effective (no significant regression in tokens-USD/unit).
4) Structured-output contracts can be validated incrementally on clients to allow partial rendering while guaranteeing eventual schema adherence.

Non-goals:
- Full replacement of existing streaming protocol (this is an ergonomic layer and optional protocol extension).
- Heavy-weight transaction semantics for multi-tool sagas (we will provide best-effort and retries; advanced saga coord belongs to Dedicated/Private playbooks).

Target personas and scenarios:
- Mobile product engineer (low-bandwidth, high-latency network). Needs to surface a one-line suggestion quickly while tool resolution can happen later.
- Web chat frontend team who wants to show early partial results and then refine with tool outputs without janky UI jumps.
- Platform engineer at mid-market customer who embeds the SDK and wants deterministic observability into tool calls and schema regressions.

Key constraints and invariants:
- Any client-side buffering must not break server-side prefix caching heuristics. SDK hints may be best-effort and should be surfaced as hints to routing/batching layer rather than hard pins.
- Tool invocations must maintain an idempotency key and a small deterministic envelope so retries and fallbacks are safe.
- Structured output validation must be incremental (partial JSON chunks, typed fields) and tolerant to later enrichment or correction.

Proposed UX / SDK Canvas (high-level):
- Session handle: lightweight object representing a conversation/interaction with configuration: latencyProfile: ["fast","balanced","accurate"], toolPolicy: ["eager-hint","defer","fire-and-forget"], schemaHints: optional typed declarations.
- sendIncremental(promptDelta, opts): app-level primitive that sends a delta. Returns an async stream of frames: {frameType, payload, confidenceHint}. Frames are small by default.
- toolHint(name, inputs, hintMode): attaches a hint to an outgoing delta. hintMode = {eager, speculative, passive}. Hints are propagated to routing to prioritize model variants that minimize tool latency and/or to pre-warm toollets.
- commitToolCall(toolCallId): explicit opt-in for blocking semantics when the UX requires the final tool result to be visible before continuing. This can convert a speculative tool hint into a required call (with increased latency).
- partialSchemaCheck(frame): returns quick PASS/FAIL/UNKNOWN for fields included in the frame; SDK surfaces lightweight corrections to UI.

Toolbound Protocol (lightweight):
- Purpose: a small wire contract that encodes tool hints, idempotency, and speculative vs required tooling flags into the request metadata and incremental frames. Designed to be compatible with our streaming transport and fall back to classic REST semantics when streaming not available.
- Minimal envelope fields (kept intentionally small): toolCalls: list of {id, name, opSigHash, inputChecksum, mode, idempotencyKey, compatibilityFlags}. All fields are short strings to avoid large metadata.
- Modes: speculative | suggested | required | background. Speculative means engine may attempt best-effort; required forces engine to wait for tool result before committing final token. Background means call can be executed asynchronously and its output attached later as a secondary frame.
- Server behavior notes: speculative toolCalls do not block token emission; required calls block emission of final qualifiers for any dependent output. The server should attempt to route required calls to low-latency tool runtimes (if the routing layer supports it) or fall back to non-blocking variants and mark the response with a toolFallback frame.

Structured output and incremental validation:
- SchemaHints: small typed descriptors (name:type pairs, required:bool) passed at session creation or per-delta. Example: [{"title":"string","steps":"array<string>","cost_est":"number?"}]. SDK will not require a full JSON object; it will allow partial frames to be validated locally.
- Incremental frames: the engine emits "patch frames" with JSON-Patch-ish fragments or typed field assignments. Clients can render partial fields and show placeholders for missing required fields.
- Validation semantics: three-state checks for each field: OK | NeedsMore | Violation. Violations are surfaced as structured telemetry and included in the evaluation pipeline so regression alerts can be raised.

SDK ergonomics examples (JS/TS pseudo):
- Fast suggestion flow (mobile):
  const session = Redwood.createSession({latencyProfile: 'fast', toolPolicy: 'eager-hint', schemaHints: {title: 'string'}})
  session.onFrame(frame => renderFrame(frame))
  session.sendIncremental({text: 'Summarize: user had issue with billing'}, {toolHint: {name: 'kb-lookup', mode: 'speculative'}})

- Blocking action (desktop UI):
  const call = session.sendIncremental({text: 'Run invoice-summary'}, {toolHint: {name: 'invoice-analyzer', mode: 'required', idempotencyKey: uuid()}})
  await call.commitToolCall() // waits for required tool result before resolving final tokens

Telemetry and observability:
- Emit per-tool-call events with: toolName, mode, routeHint, latency_ms, status (ok/fallback/error), idempotencyKey. Keep payloads small.
- Expose aggregated metrics in Console: speculativeSuccessRate, requiredLatencyP95, schemaViolationRate per model+version.

Compatibility and migration story:
- Backward compatible: clients can opt into the latency-first canvas. If a client omits toolHint metadata, server treats calls as fully implicit (existing behavior).
- Server-side feature gate: start as opt-in per-customer, then expand based on telemetry.

Evaluation plan and success metrics:
- Technical metrics: P95 first-action token latency (web/mobile), tokens-per-call cost delta, speculativeTool-success-percent (when speculative mode produced a usable tool output without commit).
- UX metrics: drop in perceived assistant latency (A/B), decreased UI jitter measured by reflow metrics when partial frames are used vs full blocking renders.
- Safety metrics: false-positive structured-output violations, tool-call idempotency failure rate.

Operational considerations and fallbacks:
- If routing cannot satisfy required calls quickly, server must emit a toolFallback frame describing reason and a recommended fallback strategy (e.g., background-execution, produce best-effort text only).
- Rate limit semantics: speculative hints should not create new quota surfaces; only committed tool calls should count against hard tool quotas. This avoids speculative prewarming causing billing surprises; we can optionally provide a prewarm credit bucket for customers who opt in.

Open questions / trade-offs (short list):
- How much metadata is safe to include per frame without regressing throughput or kernel selection heuristics? We should prototype small envelopes and measure.
- Do we provide server-side speculative execution tracing in traces to let customers debug mismatches? Likely yes, but PII considerations must be addressed.
- UX surface: is commitToolCall too heavyweight? Can we provide declarative dependencies so the engine auto-promotes speculative hints to required if downstream schema requires it?

Implementation roadmap (quarterly):
- Q1: API sketch, internal prototype using low-overhead frame envelope + server routing hints. Console telemetry stub. SDK JS/TS alpha.
- Q2: Expand server-side routing for required-tool prioritization; add mobile SDK optimizations (squeezed frames, smaller checkpoints). Early customer pilots.
- Q3: Console metrics, beta for self-serve customers, policy and quota handling for speculative pre-warm.

Quick experiments to run (engineering-friendly):
1) Envelope size vs throughput: craft three envelope sizes (tiny, medium, verbose) and run microbenchmarks on request throughput and token cost.
2) Speculative success A/B: implement speculative tool hint in a small subset of mobile sessions and measure success rate and perceived latency.
3) Partial schema rendering: instrument a web chat sample app to render partial fields and collect reflow metrics.

Next steps (near-term):
- Product: validate with two pilot customers (one mobile-first, one web chat).
- Eng: spike on tiny tool metadata envelope and measure impact on our batching kernel selection (sequence length distribution).
- SDK: implement JS/TS alpha with sendIncremental, toolHint, and a simple partialSchemaCheck API.

Notes to self / rough ideas to explore later:
- Consider a small 'prefetch credit' that customers can buy to allow speculative pre-warms without hitting tool quotas. Could be a pay-as-you-go microbundle.
- We may want an SDK helper that maps UI intent->hint patterns to reduce the chance product teams misuse modes.
- If we add automatic promotion of speculative->required, we need a clear telemetry chain to show the cost of promotions.

Appendix (short):
- Example frames (compact):
  {"frameType":"partial_field","field":"title","value":"Refund for order 3142","confidence":0.92}
  {"frameType":"tool_hint","calls":[{"id":"t1","name":"kb-lookup","mode":"speculative","idempotencyKey":"abc-123"}]}
  {"frameType":"tool_result","id":"t1","status":"ok","payloadRef":"s3://results/t1-345"}

End of draft. Feedback requested from SDK leads and serving-runtime on any kernel-level interactions we should avoid.
